newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters comments chill NZ bond market at week's end.
newsitem.headline: Peters comments chill NZ bond market at week's end.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 93.08 (PREV 93.15) 90-DAYS 6.94 (PREV 6.88)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.50 PCT (PREV 6.50) US 5-YR 6.28 (PREV 6.28)
NZ MCI -1.03 (PREV -0.94)
* NZ bond yields up after treasurer signals lower surplus, bigger bond programme
* Bank bills sold as Trade-Weighted Index weakens
* Market awaiting Thursday's budget, Friday's MPS
New Zealand bond yields closed on their highs on Friday after Treasurer Winston Peters told markets they were overly-optimistic on fiscal forecasts.
He gave a clear signal that budget surpluses would be smaller than previously signalled and the government bond tender programme will be larger than it was last year.
That sent a chill through the bond market before next Thursday's budget and Friday's Reserve Bank Monetary Policy Statement.
Peters, speaking after giving a speech to an Auckland business lunch meeting, said he felt market observers had too optimistic a view of the country's fiscal prospects ahead of next week's budget.
Asked if financial markets had been too complacent about the fiscal outlook, Peters told Reuters, "I think they have been considerably too optimistic".
One bond dealer commented: "Increasing the bond tender programme has put a few jitters up the spines of a few people in terms of the longer-term projections of the fiscal surplus.
"Is he going to let it all go down to zero again?"
The 11/06 bonds closed up seven basis points at 7.09 percent while the September 10-year futures fell 10 points to 92.80.
Expectations for the 1997/98 budget surplus had been around $2.9 billion against the Budget Policy Statement forecast of $3.3 billion, but these are now closer to $2.0 billion.
Conversely, a survey of fund managers had seen the bond tender programme at $1.0 billion but that expectation had now been raised in the market to $1.5 billion.
However, more bond issuance is not seen as a total negative with the bigger programme expected to help ensure greater liquidity.

Bank bill yields also rose but mainly in response to a weaker Trade-Weighted Index and a consequent move of the Monetary Conditions Index to over 100 basis points easier than the Reserve Bank's desired conditions stated in March.
The Reserve Bank confirmed details of the new-style monetary conditions index (MCI) it will publish when it releases its Monetary Policy Statement next Friday.
The index has been given an arbitrary base of 1000 based on the December 1996 quarter average rates of bank bills at 8.9 percent and the TWI at 67.1. Using that basis, the index closed around 820.
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
